the one entry that names the mother
THE ONE — the tree puts him in 1769

wellStreet.census: 1861, Staffordshire, Hanley, Stoke upon Trent — Wellington district, piece 1932, folio 38, schedule 22
matches: the enumerator writes GROCERS SHOP against the address
Elizabeth — and a WIDOW; Samuel was buried from Well Street in September 1855
CONFIRMED in the GRO index: Deaths, December quarter 1861, Stoke, 6b 66 — eight months after the enumerator called
the enumerator wrote 82 — eight years out, and not explained
wellStreet.caveat: The census does not say whose widow she is. It says she is James's mother, at Well Street, in a grocer's shop, a widow, born in Shropshire. The tree says Samuel Sneyd the grocer of Well Street died there in 1856 leaving a widow Elizabeth Margaret Oliver, born at Oswestry in Shropshire, who died in Staffordshire on 1 December 1861. Those are two independent statements that agree on the street, the shop, the widowhood, the forename and the county, and that place her death eight months after the enumerator called. No parish entry names her as Samuel's wife in this archive yet, so this is an identification, not a record.
wellStreet.birthplace: Her birthplace is transcribed “Staly Cladwin”, Shropshire. No Shropshire parish is spelled that way, and Oswestry — where the tree puts her — is not a plausible reading of it. Oswestry's neighbours include names that a bad hand could turn into this, but naming one would be inventing evidence. It is recorded here exactly as the transcriber read it.
wellStreet.ageProblem: One number does not fit. Born 1787, she is seventy-three in April 1861; the enumerator wrote EIGHTY-TWO. Ages on a census are what somebody in the house said on the night, and eighty-two for seventy-three is a large error — but it is the kind of error an eighty-year-old household makes about its oldest member, and it is the only figure on the page that argues against the identification. It is printed here rather than quietly dropped.

coverage1861: FreeCEN holds 1861 for Staffordshire and, on testing, nothing else: a control search for John Smith born 1800–1805 in Staffordshire returns 31 people and every one of them is 1861. So Samuel Sneyd, who died in 1856, could never have appeared however hard he was looked for — and his son Samuel Charles had been in Australia for twenty-four years.

burial.reg: Hanley, St John the Evangelist · parish register, entry 2330

index.what: General Register Office death index, via FreeBMD
index.entry: Deaths, September quarter 1855 — SNEYD, Samuel — Stoke upon Trent — volume 6b, page 75
index.window: Searched for every Samuel Sneyd death registered anywhere in England and Wales between March 1854 and December 1858. There is exactly one.

widow.what: General Register Office death index, via FreeBMD
widow.entry: Deaths, December quarter 1861 — SNEYD, Elizabeth — Stoke upon Trent — volume 6b, page 66

death.tree: Samuel Sneyd, born 1769 at Madeley, “a grocer of Hanley”, died 20 September 1856 at No 3, Well St, Hanley.
verdict: CONFIRMED — and the register gives the number as 91, not 3
WRONG. He was buried on 23 September 1855, and the only Samuel Sneyd death registered in England and Wales in five years is the September quarter of 1855 at Stoke
CONSISTENT. A death on the 20th and a burial on the 23rd is an ordinary three-day interval; it is the year that is out, not the date
The register says 77, which puts his birth about 1778
CONFIRMED — Deaths, December quarter 1861, Sneyd Elizabeth, Stoke, 6b 66
death.age: Seventy-seven in September 1855 means born about 1778. The tree's 1769 would make him eighty-seven — ten years adrift. The Madeley baptism this archive corrected to in the first place, Samuel son of William Sneyd the weaver and Mary Blackbourne, 4 June 1781, would make him seventy-four: three years out, which is what a stated age at burial normally is. The burial register was found long after that correction was made and it independently supports it.
death.closing: So a claim that had no record behind it three days ago now has three: a burial with an age and a house number, a death registration with a volume and page, and a census that finds his widow in the same street six years later. Two details in it were wrong, and both are the kind that a family tree gets wrong — a year, and a street number.

census1851.ref: 1851 census · WELL STREET, Hanley, Stoke upon Trent · HO107/2004, folio 138, page 13, schedule 46
census1851.means: Four years before he died, Samuel Sneyd is in his own shop in Well Street, a GROCER, born at MADELEY — and his wife Elizabeth is beside him, born at OSWESTRY, SHROPSHIRE. Every element of the tree's claim, and every element of the identification this archive made from the 1861 census, is confirmed at once by a record that names them both.

fmp.staly: And it settles “Staly Cladwin”. The 1861 enumerator wrote something at Well Street that the transcriber could not read and rendered as a Shropshire place that does not exist. The 1851 enumerator, ten years earlier, wrote OSWESTRY.

oliver.ref: Shropshire Baptisms · Oswestry, St Oswald's · Shropshire Archives P214/A/2/1, page 18
oliver.line: ELIZABETH OLIVER, born 17 MAY 1782, baptised 19 May 1782 · father DAVID Oliver, mother MARY
oliver.tree: The tree says Elizabeth Margaret Oliver, born 7 May 1787 at Oswestry.
oliver.reading: Oswestry is confirmed outright by the 1851 census. The day differs by one digit (7 for 17) and the year by one (1787 for 1782), and both censuses put her birth nearer 1780 than 1787 — 71 in 1851, 82 in 1861. She is the only Elizabeth Oliver baptised at Oswestry in the window the censuses point to, in a parish whose baptisms are thoroughly indexed. It is very probably her, and it is an identification rather than a proof.
oliver.new: It also gives a generation this archive has never had: DAVID OLIVER and MARY, of Oswestry.

audlem.claim: The tree says Samuel Sneyd married Elizabeth Margaret Oliver at AUDLEM, CHESHIRE on 22 October 1809.
audlem.test: Audlem's registers are indexed twice over — Cheshire Diocese of Chester Parish Marriages AND the Bishop's Transcripts. A control search for SMITH marrying at Audlem between 1804 and 1814 returns twenty entries from both collections.
audlem.result: No Sneyd, in any spelling, marries at Audlem in that window. Widening to every Sneyd record at Audlem of any date and any type returns thirty-six results and every one is a civil registration after 1837 from Nantwich, Crewe or Congleton. Not one Sneyd appears in Audlem's parish registers at all.
audlem.verdict: So the Audlem marriage is not supported. That is not the same as disproved — a mangled spelling or a licence elsewhere would explain it — but it has now been looked for properly, against a parish that is covered twice, and it is not there.

fmp.ages: One thing moves. The tree gives Samuel's birth as 1769 and this archive corrected that to the Madeley baptism of 4 June 1781. The 1851 census says he was 72, so born about 1779; the burial register said 77 in September 1855, so about 1778. Three records now cluster around 1778–79, which sits between the tree's 1769 and the archive's 1781 and matches neither exactly. The Madeley baptism remains the best candidate — it has the right father, mother, parish and trade — but the ages do not endorse it as cleanly as they rule out 1769.

wellStreetYears.head: Sixty years in one street
rows: SAMUEL SNEYD, 72, grocer, born Madeley · Elizabeth his wife, 71, born Oswestry · James, 33, engraver · Elizabeth Ann, 11
Samuel buried from this address, 23 September, aged 77
Hanley St John the Evangelist, entry 2330
JAMES SNEYD, 42, engraver · Ann his wife, 41 · Elizabeth A 21 and Mary J 18, both PAINTRESSES · James A, 10 · and Elizabeth, 82, WIDOW, born Shropshire
James, 53, engraver · Ann, 52 · James A, 20, ENGRAVER
James, 63, ENGRAVER (POTTER) · Anne, 61 · Mary Elizabeth MULLOCK (Sneyd), granddaughter, 17, dressmaker
wellStreetYears.means: Samuel Charles Sneyd sailed for New South Wales in 1832 and died at Brisbane in 1885. His brother James stayed in Well Street and engraved pottery there for the rest of his life — thirty years on from his father's shop, in the same road, with his own son at the same trade. Two sons of one grocer, and the whole distance of the nineteenth century between them.
wellStreetYears.mullock: The granddaughter of 1881 is entered as Mary Elizabeth MULLOCK (Sneyd), born Hanley about 1864 — so one of the paintress daughters of 1861 married a Mullock. A thread this archive has not followed.

williamBurial.head: And the weaver himself has a burial at last — or one of two
williamBurial.body: The Sneyd line's oldest name is WILLIAM SNEYD OF MADELEY, and until today he rested on a citation reading “Sneyd Web Site”, a birth year of 1746, AND NO DEATH AT ALL. The National Burial Index holds eight William Sneyds buried at MADELEY ALL SAINTS across two hundred and fifty years — 1574, 1640, 1659, 1762, 1780, 1791, and then two that matter:
rows: He would have been 38 at the weaver's marriage and 63 at the last of his children. Possible, and old.
He would have been 26 at the marriage and 51 at the last child — the natural fit, and within three years of the 1746 the tree gives him.
williamBurial.means: The weaver married about April 1769 — the first child is baptised three months later — and was still fathering children in 1794, so neither of the 1780 nor 1791 burials can be him. That leaves TWO CANDIDATES, and this page is not going to pick one and call it settled. The 1827 burial fits far better on every measure. What it is NOT is proof: the register names no wife, no trade and no children, and two men of one name in one parish is exactly the situation that has caught this archive before.
williamBurial.gain: What has changed is the shape of the problem. Yesterday the oldest Sneyd was a web page. Today he is one of two documented burials in the right parish, with ages, and the better of the two agrees with the tree to within three years — which is what a stated age at burial does.

wills.head: Thirty-six Sneyd wills, and a labourer at Keele
wills.lede: The Diocese of Lichfield and Coventry wills index, 1550–1810, is free and this archive had never opened it. It returns thirty-six Sneyds. Not one of them is of MADELEY.
wills.where: Staffordshire Name Indexes, staffsnameindexes.org.uk, searched 14 September 2026. The site indexes twenty-six collections but NOT parish registers or bishop's transcripts, so it cannot answer the Madeley burials directly.
wills.keeleHead: What it does to the Keele graft

labourer.head: A labourer with a will, in the squires' own parish
labourer.body: Four Ralph Sneyds of Keele, esquires and gentlemen, across forty years — and in 1772, RICHARD SNEYD, LABOURER, of Keele, leaving a will in the same court.
labourer.means: This archive has an open question it calls the Keele graft: whether its own Sneyds were attached to the Sneyds of Keele Hall by someone who wanted a better ancestor. The labourer cuts the question loose from the answer. Being a Sneyd of Keele does not make a man gentry, because in 1772 a Sneyd of Keele was a labourer. A humble Sneyd in that parish needs no descent from the squires to explain him.
labourer.chip: it weakens the graft without disproving it
labourer.careful: It is not evidence that this archive's Sneyds were the labouring sort, and it is not evidence that they were at Keele at all. It removes an assumption, which is the most a negative can do.

madeley.head: And nothing at Madeley
madeley.body: Sneyd of Madeley returns nothing in an index of thirty-six Sneyd wills spanning two hundred and sixty years. The control is the same search without a place, which returns all thirty-six, so the engine and the surname both work.
madeley.means: The Madeley burials remain a question for the Lichfield bishop's transcripts, which this index does not hold and which nothing free does.

wills.potteries: The rest cluster where this archive already knew to look: yeomen at Woodhead in Burslem in 1707 and 1717, a gentleman at The Birches, Burslem in 1708, a spinster at Woodhead in 1722, a wheelwright at Newcastle under Lyme in 1676. The Potteries, two generations before the potteries.

biddulph.head: Ann has a surname at last
biddulph.lede: Four censuses give James Sneyd the engraver a wife called ANN and nothing more — Ann, 41, in 1861; Ann, 52, in 1871; Anne, 61, in 1881. The free Staffordshire index names her.
biddulph.marriage: SNEYD, James · married ANN BIDDULPH · 1842 · STOKE, ST PETER · reference 31/03/214
biddulph.kidsHead: And it names four children, by their mother's maiden name
biddulph.kidsNote: The Staffordshire birth index records the MOTHER'S MAIDEN NAME beside every child. Four Sneyd births carry BIDDULPH:
kids: the “Mary J, 18” of 1861, a PAINTRESS — and her full name for the first time
NEW. She is in no census this archive has read; she did not survive to 1851, or she was elsewhere on both nights
the “James A, 10” of 1861 and the “James A, 20, ENGRAVER” of 1871 — his full name too
biddulph.means: Three of the four match the household this archive already had, and two of them supply the forenames the censuses gave only as initials. The district is right — Shelton and Hanley are the two halves of the ground around Well Street. The identification rests on a surname, a maiden name repeated across four entries, a district and four matching ages, which is as much as an index can carry.
biddulph.chipMeans: identified from an index, not from a certificate
biddulph.orderHead: And one detail the index states plainly
biddulph.order: Elizabeth Ann was born in 1839. The marriage is 1842. The eldest child came three years before the wedding, and the registrar recorded her under her father's surname with her mother's maiden name beside it, which is exactly how the index is built to work.
biddulph.careful: What would settle it is the marriage certificate, which would give both fathers' names and occupations and carry this line back a generation on Ann's side. Against the local reference 31/03/214 it is orderable from Stoke-on-Trent rather than from the GRO.
biddulph.where: Searched 15 September 2026 at staffordshirebmd.org.uk — 391 Sneyd births and 322 Sneyd marriages, free, and never used by this archive before.

biddulphParents.head: Ann's parents, and the night the family slept in two houses
biddulphParents.found: 16 September 2026, the first hour of a FindMyPast subscription
biddulphParents.lede: This archive knew James Sneyd's wife as «Ann» across four censuses, then as ANN BIDDULPH from a free index, and said plainly that her parents were a generation it had never had. The 1851 census names them.

queen.head: Queen Street, Stoke upon Trent — seven people

well.head: And Well Street, the same night — five people

biddulphParents.means: **JOHN BIDDULPH, coal dealer, born at Bermondsey in Surrey about 1798, and JULIA his wife, born at Shelton about 1799.** Ann is enumerated in their house as «Daughter, Married», a dressmaker of 31, with two of her own children beside her as grandchildren. Her husband James is a mile away at his father's shop in Well Street with their eldest, Elizabeth Ann. On the night of 30 March 1851 this family slept at two addresses, and it takes both to see it whole.
biddulphParents.nameHead: And the naming falls into place
biddulphParents.name: James and Ann called their second daughter **MARY JULIA** in 1842. Ann's mother is **JULIA** and her sister is **MARY**. Their eldest was **ELIZABETH ANN** — for James's mother Elizabeth and for Ann herself. The forenames this archive had been reading as decoration are a map of the two families.
biddulphParents.surrey: John Biddulph was born at **Bermondsey, Surrey** — not in Staffordshire at all. A coal dealer in the Potteries who came up from south London is a different kind of ancestor from a local family, and nothing here explains how he got there. His marriage to Julia, and his own parents, are the next question and are not yet asked.
